questions_asked: Do reports of a new hornet sighting arrive as a steady, even trickle, or in sudden bursts after news spreads and people start looking?
When the lab confirms a report, what single thing makes them most confident it really is the giant hornet?
If your model ranks reports to investigate, how wrong can it be before you'd stop trusting it?
expert_answers:
Bursts, not a steady trickle. Public-report data of this kind is strongly event-driven: submission volume spikes sharply after media coverage, official announcements, nest discoveries/destructions, or the start of the seasonal "hornet watch" period, then decays. The 2019 Vancouver Island nest news and subsequent Washington confirmations are exactly the kind of trigger that produces clustered arrivals.

Two practical consequences for the model: (1) report arrivals are not well described by a constant-rate (Poisson) process — expect overdispersion and clustering, so a non-homogeneous or self-exciting (Hawkes-type) process is more appropriate; (2) the submission date, not the detection date, carries the burst signal, and the lag between them is itself informative. This is an empirical judgment about reporting behavior, not a precise figure.

The single strongest confidence signal is a clear, close-up photograph (or physical specimen) showing the diagnostic features unique to *Vespa mandarinia* — most reliably the massive orange/yellow head with large prominent eyes and the distinctive broad orange-and-black banded abdomen — ideally with a size reference. A confirmed specimen or an unambiguous image beats any written description, because text notes are subjective and often describe generic "big hornet" features shared by look-alikes.

There is no universal numeric threshold; it depends on the base rate and the cost asymmetry. In this dataset positives are rare (on the order of a few percent of reports), so a ranking model is only useful if it concentrates positives far above that base rate in the top-ranked tier.

Practical judgment: I would stop trusting the ranking when its top-decile (or top-N) precision falls to roughly the base rate — i.e., when investigating the highest-ranked reports is no better than picking at random. As a working rule, a model that cannot lift precision to at least several times the base rate in the tier you actually have resources to investigate is not worth acting on. Also stop trusting it if precision is unstable across time or geography (it may be fitting the news-burst artifact rather than hornet features), or if its errors are systematically the costly kind — false negatives on genuine positives.

These are empirical judgments about acceptable performance, not fixed figures.
